newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia gov't agrees deal with striking workers.
newsitem.headline: Colombia gov't agrees deal with striking workers.

text.p: Colombian government ministers and union leaders agreed a pay hike worth as much as 20 percent for state workers Monday evening, opening the way for an imminent end to a seven-day-old public sector strike.
Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo, spearheading the government's efforts to rein in a burgeoning fiscal deficit, said the deal would cost the nation 115 billion pesos.

There has been little headway on union demands for the government to shelve plans for a wave of privatizations of national and regional industries but hopes were high a full deal would be worked out within the next few hours.
"There have been significant advances but there's still nothing final. I expect we will have some agreement in a few hours," said Hernando Hernndez, head of the main oil workers' union USO.
An estimated 800,000 state workers launched an indefinite strike at midnight last Monday to press for a 21.5 percent pay hike, compared to the government offer of a weighted 13.5 percent.

Under the terms of the deal agreed Monday, state workers receiving the equivalent of between one and two minimum salaries will get a full 20 percent raise. The increase will 18 percent for those earning three or four minimum wages. The minimum wage until Dec. 31 last year stood at about $140 per month.

For higher paid public sector workers the salary increase will be range between eight and 16 percent. Despite the additional cost implications of the pay deal Ocampo told reporters he was confident the government would meet its target of slashing back the 1997 budget by 1.3 trillion pesos.

Union demands for a review of legal action facing oil workers and employees of the state phone company Telecom were agreed earlier in the day together with a government pledge that strikers would not face sanctions on their return to work.

Hernndez said as soon as a deal was reached to lift the nationwide public sector work stoppage the USO would restart collective contract negotiations with the state-run oil company Ecopetrol in a bid to avert a threatened shut down of the state oil industry.

The impact of the seven-day strike has been hard to judge. President Ernesto Samper claimed just 10 percent of public employees heeded the strike call while union chiefs said they had severely disrupted key economic and social sectors.
